data.hypothesis: The measured two-group schedule was slower than baseline (82.32 µs versus 55.00 µs), while the measured four-group schedule was also slower but less so (63.81 µs). A three-group scalar unroll tests whether intermediate lookup concurrency reduces loop overhead without the four-group schedule's larger live-value set; register pressure and the combined validity check may still outweigh any benefit.

memory_lessons.applicability: Scalar table-loop unrolling on this base64 workload.
memory_lessons.claim: The two-group and four-group scalar candidates were both correct but slower than the measured baseline; the four-group candidate was faster than the two-group candidate, but neither establishes a speedup over baseline.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure the three-group schedule on the same protocol, including lengths and padding cases near its 24-character bulk boundary.

data.notes: This is a three-group (24 input characters, 18 output bytes) scalar scheduling contrast, reserving one quartet for the unchanged scalar tail. The two-group result (82.32 µs) and four-group result (63.81 µs) were both correct but slower than the 55.00 µs baseline; these are prior measurements, not results for this candidate. No local validation or timing was performed; the controller should run correctness checks for empty/short inputs, group-boundary lengths, padding, random valid inputs, and Lena before repeated native timing.
transformations: Unrolled the table-driven decode loop to process three independent eight-character groups per bulk iteration, interleaving scalar lookups across groups.
Required at least 28 remaining input characters before processing 24, reserving a quartet for scalar padding, tail, and invalid-input handling.
Used one combined validity check before stores so invalid blocks fall through to the existing scalar decoder without changing output semantics.
Added no explicit SIMD, parallel execution, benchmark-length specialization, or changes outside src/candidate.cpp.
